Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome

glomerular or not, then symptomatic or not · nephritis weeks after strep: complement and volumeIs it glomerular, how long since the infection, is complement low, and is the child overloaded?

Glomerular or notNephritic syndromePractice
Bottom line

With dysuria, leukocyte esterase and pyuria, the blood is part of the cystitis, not a separate workup. Otherwise ask in order: is it glomerular, and if not, does a symptom name the cause?

  • Glomerular hematuria: any of brown, tea or cola urine, red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, protein, edema or hypertension; check creatinine, complement levels and a complete blood count (CBC).
  • Non-glomerular hematuria: bright red urine or clots, normal red cell shape, no protein. With no symptom to name the cause: renal and bladder ultrasound, the first image for painless gross hematuria, since a young child's kidney stone is often painless; urine culture; and a spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio for hypercalciuria, a common cause of asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross, in a well child.
  • Nephritic syndrome: hematuria with red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, hypertension, edema, oliguria and a rising creatinine; protein present but usually below the nephrotic range.
  • Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN): begins about 2 to 4 weeks after a strep throat or skin infection. Hematuria during or within days of an upper respiratory infection is immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy.
  • Complement clock: C3 (complement component 3) low at onset, back to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks; still low after 8 weeks suggests a different lesion.

Nephritic syndrome after strep
Acute nephritis in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness script and tellAgainst it 2 weeks after a sore throat
PSGNImmune complexes after group A strep pharyngitis or impetigo; edema, hypertension, cola urine; weeks later, low C3, normal by 6 to 8 weeks; positive ASO or anti-DNase B; children recover over weeksThe answer
IgA nephropathyMesangial IgA; recurrent gross hematuria in an older child or young adult, during or within days of an infection; normal C3Two-week gap; edema and hypertension, not isolated episodes
IgA vasculitis nephritisSmall-vessel IgA vasculitis; kidney disease can follow the rash by weeks; palpable purpura on legs and buttocks, arthritis, abdominal pain; normal C3No rash, joint or abdominal pain
Lupus nephritis or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)Immune-complex nephritis that does not resolve; lupus mostly in adolescent girls; persistently low complement; lupus lowers C3 and C4 (complement component 4), with a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA)Decided at 8 weeks: an unrecovered C3 calls for further investigation, including a biopsy
Alport syndromeType IV collagen defect, usually X-linked; persistent hematuria with sensorineural hearing loss and family kidney failure; slow progressionAcute onset after an infection; no deafness or family history
Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)Shiga toxin after bloody diarrhea; microangiopathy; hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, low platelets plus acute kidney injury (AKI)Normal blood count; sore throat, not diarrhea
Practice
  1. 6-year-old boy has bright red urine since yesterday No dysuria, trauma or recent infection no edema or flank tenderness BP 100/65 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts; leukocyte esterase and nitrite negative → Renal and bladder ultrasonography → bright red urine with no protein, casts, edema or hypertension is nonglomerular, and no symptom names a cause. In a young child a kidney stone is often painless and sitting in the kidney, so it presents as gross hematuria alone; the ultrasound finds many stones and any obstruction with no radiation and also excludes a renal mass such as Wilms tumor. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, which is very rare in children. Noncontrast CT is more sensitive for small stones but carries radiation, so in a child it follows a nondiagnostic ultrasound
  2. 8-year-old boy has 2 days of tea-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago, resolved without treatment puffy eyelids; mild pretibial edema urine: red cell casts, 2+ protein BP 140/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → a latent period of weeks, not days, with red cell casts, protein and hypertension: expect a low C3 that normalizes by 6 to 8 weeks and a positive ASO or anti-DNase B. IgA nephropathy bleeds during or within days of an upper respiratory infection with a normal C3. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is the nephritis that does not resolve, with a persistently low complement; it is raised when the C3 is still low at 8 weeks
  3. 8-year-old girl was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis yesterday periorbital and pedal edema Her physician considers drugs for her blood pressure BP 150/96 mm Hg · creatinine 1.7 mg/dL · potassium 6.0 mEq/L → Lisinopril → ACE inhibitors raise potassium and can lower the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in AKI, and this potassium is already high. Furosemide treats the overload that drives the edema and pressure, and nifedipine follows if pressure stays high after diuresis
  4. 14-year-old boy receiving cyclophosphamide has 2 days of bright red urine with clots suprapubic discomfort; no flank pain Urine culture shows no growth Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · urine: protein negative, no casts → Hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein → bright red urine with clots on cyclophosphamide is a hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein, which mesna and hydration given with the drug help prevent. After a transplant, think of BK (a polyomavirus) or adenovirus. A bacterial cystitis needs significant bacteriuria on culture, and bladder cancer is very rare in children
  5. 7-year-old girl has microscopic hematuria on two routine urinalyses Well, with no dysuria, flank pain or edema urine: no protein, no casts, normal red cell shape BP 98/60 mm Hg · urine culture negative · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL → Urine calcium/creatinine ratio → hypercalciuria is a common cause of asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross, in a well child and the main risk factor for a stone; a high spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio finds it. A biopsy is a glomerular test, and this urine has no protein, casts, edema or hypertension. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, very rare in children
  6. 16-year-old boy has a third episode of cola-colored urine each began 1 to 2 days into a sore throat Between episodes he feels well urine: red cells, 1+ protein BP 118/74 mm Hg · C3 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → IgA nephropathy → synpharyngitic hematuria, within 1 to 2 days of the sore throat, recurrent, with a normal C3: mesangial IgA, typical in an older child or young adult. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis comes 2 to 4 weeks after the infection, with a low C3. Thin basement membrane disease usually presents as isolated microscopic hematuria; gross bleeds occur in only a minority, often after infection
  7. 9-year-old boy has headache, lethargy and 2 days of low urine output Sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital, scrotal and pedal edema; no rash BP 170/102 mm Hg, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, normal blood count · urine: moderate blood, 2+ protein → Furosemide → hematuria with protein, hypertension, edema and a rising creatinine two weeks after a sore throat is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains salt and water, and the edema and hypertension both come from that volume: the first drug is a loop diuretic, with sodium and fluid restriction. Saline answers the low urine output and raised creatinine, but this child is overloaded, not dry. Plasmapheresis treats antibody-mediated anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease; this disease is immune-complex and self-limited. Headache and lethargy at this pressure are signs of hypertensive encephalopathy, so a calcium channel blocker is added alongside the diuretic now rather than after diuresis; it is not among these options
  8. 68-year-old man has two episodes of painless bright red urine Smokes one pack daily for 45 years no dysuria or flank pain Afebrile · BP 136/84 mm Hg · urine: over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein, casts or leukocyte esterase → Cystoscopy + CT urography → painless gross hematuria in an older adult or smoker earns CT urography and cystoscopy, which find a mass or stone; bladder cancer is the concern at this age. A repeat urinalysis in weeks delays that, and a renal ultrasound alone skips the cystoscopy and detects far fewer upper tract urothelial tumors than CT urography
  9. 10-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 3 months ago Seen at a scheduled follow-up visit edema has resolved microscopic hematuria persists on urinalysis BP 108/68 mm Hg · C3 still low · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL → Renal biopsy → a C3 that has not recovered by 8 weeks calls for further investigation, including a biopsy, to look for membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis. Microscopic hematuria may persist for up to 5 years, but C3 returns to normal within 6 to 8 weeks in about 80%; waiting 3 more months delays the biopsy, and a repeat ASO shows only recent strep infection, not why the C3 stays low
  10. 8-year-old boy has had 3 days of tea-colored urine He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital edema urine: red cell casts, 1+ protein Afebrile · BP 138/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Serum C3 level → nephritis weeks after pharyngitis: a low C3 with a normal or mildly low C4 supports poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis; a normal C3 means IgA nephropathy or IgA vasculitis, and a low C3 and C4 suggest lupus. A biopsy is generally only for an atypical course (C3 still low after 8 weeks or worsening), and an ultrasound shows size and structure, not immune complexes
  11. 10-year-old boy has microscopic hematuria on every urinalysis since age 4 sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry His maternal uncle had kidney failure at 30 BP 112/70 mm Hg · urine: 1+ protein · C3 normal → Alport syndrome → persistent hematuria with sensorineural hearing loss and a family history of kidney failure is a type IV collagen defect, usually X-linked, progressing slowly to kidney failure. Thin basement membrane disease does not bring deafness. IgA nephropathy bleeds in recurrent gross episodes during or within days of an upper respiratory infection
  12. 11-year-old boy fell onto bicycle handlebars 3 hours ago left flank pain, bruising; bright red urine alert; abdomen soft, left flank tender HR 96/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · large blood, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts → Contrast CT of the abdomen → hematuria after abdominal or flank trauma: CT shows and stages the renal injury. Ultrasound may be used in children, but CT is preferred, and waiting a week to repeat the urinalysis leaves the injury unstaged
  13. 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 2 days ago headache After 24 hours of furosemide with sodium and fluid restriction alert, no respiratory distress BP 165/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.8 mEq/L → Add nifedipine → pressure that stays high after 24 hours of diuresis is the indication for a calcium channel blocker, so waiting another day is not the step. Watch for hypertensive encephalopathy: headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures. Dialysis is for refractory overload, hyperkalemia or uremia, none of which is present
  14. 17-year-old girl has 5 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner; no fever or flank pain urine: leukocyte esterase positive, 20 white cells/hpf, a few red cells urine culture: no growth Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT → sterile pyuria with dysuria in a sexually active adolescent: test for chlamydia and gonorrhea with a nucleic acid amplification test. Other causes of sterile pyuria are renal tuberculosis, interstitial nephritis, a partially treated urinary tract infection and appendicitis. A culture for bacterial cystitis already grew nothing, which is what makes this pyuria sterile, and a renal ultrasound answers flank pain with crystals or painless gross hematuria
  15. 6-year-old girl has cola-colored urine and puffy eyelids Crusted sores on her legs 4 weeks ago red cell casts; no rash or joint pain BP 138/90 mm Hg · C3 low · C4 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → nephritis about 2 to 4 weeks after a strep skin infection, with a low C3 and normal C4, a C3 expected to normalize within 8 weeks; anti-DNase B is the better strep marker after impetigo. IgA nephropathy bleeds within days of an infection with a normal C3, and IgA vasculitis brings palpable purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain with a normal C3
  16. 9-year-old girl has 2 days of brown urine puffy eyelids each morning mild pretibial edema BP 132/86 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, protein 2+, red cell casts · no leukocyte esterase or nitrite → Serum creatinine, complement levels and CBC → brown urine with protein, casts, edema and hypertension is glomerular hematuria: check creatinine, complement levels and a CBC. A low C3 after a recent strep infection points to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The ultrasound and calcium/creatinine ratio belong to the nonglomerular branch
How NBME framed it: question 1

8-year-old girl with 6 days of intermittent headache, tiredness and little appetite, then 2 days of brown urine Vomited yesterday morning; no abdominal pain, diarrhea or dysuria Sore throat and fever 2 weeks ago that cleared without treatment; previously healthy, no medications; normal growth and development mildly pale, not distressed; height 50th percentile, weight 75th T 36.7 °C · HR 108/min · respiratory rate 16/min · BP 138/88 mm Hg large, mildly red tonsils without exudate; lungs clear grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, no rub or gallop; abdomen normal; warm extremities with 1+ edema serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL · urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL · sodium 132 mEq/L · potassium 5.2 mEq/L · chloride 100 mEq/L · bicarbonate 15 mEq/L urine: blood 2+ · protein 1+ · red cell casts too numerous to count · pH 5 · specific gravity 1.020 · Gram stain: no organisms

Most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Antinuclear antibody assay: pulls toward lupus nephritis; but ANA is neither sensitive nor specific for PSGN, and lupus would lower both C3 and C4.
  • Urine culture: the urine is abnormal; but a culture answers a urinary tract infection; there is no dysuria and the Gram stain shows no organisms.
  • Renal ultrasonography: the creatinine is rising; but immune-complex deposits are microscopic, not visible on ultrasound.

Down to two: serum C3 or echocardiography. Serum C3: brown urine with casts, protein, hypertension and edema 2 weeks after a sore throat; deposited immune complexes consume C3, so the serum level falls. The soft ejection murmur after the sore throat baits rheumatic carditis, but the lungs are clear, so heart failure is unlikely.

Management ladder for PSGN Volume overload – inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains salt and water; edema and hypertension both come from that volume; headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures mean hypertensive encephalopathy · Every child – supportive care with sodium and fluid restriction · Loop diuretic – furosemide first, for edema or hypertension from volume overload; saline for the oliguria would worsen it · Calcium channel blocker – nifedipine when pressure stays high after diuresis or encephalopathy appears; ACE inhibitors only with caution in AKI because of hyperkalemia · Dialysis – refractory overload, hyperkalemia or uremia · No role – plasmapheresis, since the disease is self-limited · Antibiotics – treat a still-active strep infection but do not change the renal course
Nitrite is only about 50% sensitive It needs a nitrate-reducing organism (Enterococcus, S. saprophyticus and Pseudomonas are not) and adequate bladder dwell time. A negative nitrite never excludes a urinary tract infection when leukocyte esterase, pyuria and symptoms agree.
Painless gross hematuria in a child A kidney stone in a young child is often painless and sitting in the kidney, so it presents as gross hematuria alone, and crystals are not always seen. Hypercalciuria is the main risk factor: look for earlier microscopic hematuria and a high spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio. The renal and bladder ultrasound comes first; noncontrast CT only if it is nondiagnostic. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, which is very rare in children. Meatal irritation is painful and visible on exam: reassure.
Course Nephritis days after an upper respiratory infection is IgA nephropathy; weeks after pharyngitis or impetigo, PSGN. Treating strep pharyngitis promptly prevents rheumatic fever but does not reliably prevent PSGN. Children usually recover fully within weeks, although microscopic hematuria may persist for up to 5 years; adults are more likely to develop chronic kidney disease.
Common wrong answers A negative nitrite overruling leukocyte esterase, pyuria and symptoms. Cystoscopy in a child: right for an older adult, but bladder cancer is very rare in a 6-year-old, so the ultrasound comes first. Noncontrast CT before the ultrasound: more sensitive for small stones, but radiation. A 24-hour urine protein or kidney biopsy for bright red urine with no protein, casts, edema or hypertension. Normal saline for a low urine output in an overloaded child. Plasmapheresis: treats antibody-mediated anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; PSGN is immune-complex and self-limited. Lisinopril first: risks hyperkalemia in AKI; diuresis first, then a calcium channel blocker. Protein restriction: for chronic kidney disease, not a self-limited acute nephritis.
Pairs with Part I Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child: protein without red cells, from the well child’s routine dipstick to the young child with periorbital edema who gets steroids without a biopsy. Ask: does the urine show red cells and casts, or protein alone? Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes starts one step earlier: is the swelling local to the eye? Part I Acute Kidney Injury in a Child: the AKI that does need fluids. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child sends the renal involvement of IgA vasculitis here. Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia: HUS.
Transferable rule

With a full lab panel, base the diagnosis on the pattern of the panel, not the most alarming single value; a discordant component reflects a test's limited sensitivity and does not overrule the pattern. In a child with AKI, decide whether the kidney needs volume given or removed before choosing a drug: edema with hypertension means overload, so the loop diuretic comes first and saline is harmful.
